summary: Switzerland is not in the EU but joins the Schengen Area through association agreements: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (the ETIAS travel authorization is not yet in operation), and everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Where the application is lodged with an external service provider, as at most Swiss representations, the provider's service fee is payable on top.

fee.notes: The Swiss-franc equivalent of EUR 90 (EUR 45 for children aged 6–12; free under 6), collected in the currency the Swiss representation sets. For stays over 90 days (residence, family reunification); requires prior authorization from the cantonal migration authority.

fee.notes: The Swiss-franc equivalent of EUR 90 (EUR 45 for children aged 6–12; free under 6), collected in the currency the Swiss representation sets. For courses longer than 90 days; the cantonal migration authority must approve the stay before the visa is issued. Proof of enrollment, funds and accommodation required. Holders of scholarships from the federal institutes of technology, the Federal Scholarship Commission or the Swiss National Science Foundation get the visa free of charge.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU/EFTA passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000 (roughly CHF 28,000–30,000), valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it, but Swiss healthcare is expensive — cover is strongly recommended.

source.instrument: Regulation (EC) No 810/2009 establishing a Community Code on Visas, Article 15(3) — travel medical insurance with minimum coverage of EUR 30 000

source.name: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) — FAQ Entry

proofOfFunds.text: Third-country visitors staying at their own expense must be able to show at least CHF 100 per day of their stay (CHF 30 for students with a valid student permit), in cash, cards or bank statements if asked.

source.name: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) — FAQ Entry

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Switzerland participates in the EU Entry/Exit System as a Schengen associate: non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) at Schengen external borders, including Swiss airports. Registration happens at the border. Allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: ETIAS will also apply to Switzerland as a Schengen associate: visa-exempt travelers will need the authorization to enter. It is not yet in operation, and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. Check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Unlike the EU, Switzerland has no obligation to declare cash. However, customs officers can ask anyone carrying CHF 10,000 or more (or equivalent) about their identity and the origin, intended use and beneficial owner of the money — refusing to answer or giving false information is an offense, and the amount is recorded.

payments.text: No official source we could read describes card acceptance in Switzerland. The currency is the Swiss franc (CHF).

safety.text: Switzerland is one of the safest countries in the world, with very low crime. Petty theft can occur around train stations and tourist sights; in the mountains, the main risks are weather and terrain. Check conditions before hiking.

bestTimeToVisit.text: No official seasonal guidance. The UK FCDO notes that alpine winters make driving difficult (winter tyres and snow chains needed), that avalanches are a risk during heavy snow, and that there is a heightened risk of wildfires in summer.

roadVignette.appliesTo: All motor vehicles and trailers up to 3.5 t; a towed trailer needs its own vignette.

penalty.notes: Fine for using a motorway without a valid vignette (or with one not properly affixed); you must also buy a vignette or register the plate for the e-vignette on the spot. A car and trailer that both lack one are fined twice. Non-residents who dispute it or do not pay at once must leave a deposit.

source.name: FOCBS — Guideline R-15-01 National road charge (motorway vignette)

roadVignette.text: Switzerland sells exactly one vignette: CHF 40, valid for 14 months from December 1 of the previous year to January 31 of the following one. There are no short-term options, so a single motorway trip costs the full CHF 40. You can choose the e-vignette linked to your number plate (e-vignette.ch) or the sticker on the windscreen; both cost the same. Buy it before entering the country — only at Basel St. Louis, Rheinfelden and Kreuzlingen may you use the motorway without one, and only as far as the first exit.

source.name: Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS) — Motorway charge FAQ

tips.text: The 90-day limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, not just Switzerland — days spent in France or Italy count against the same allowance.

Driving on Swiss motorways requires a vignette (CHF 40, as a sticker or e-vignette). The UK FCDO says you can buy one at most border crossings, petrol stations, post offices or online, and that driving without one can bring a large fine; Canada notes rental cars are generally equipped with one.
Switzerland uses type C and type J plugs (IEC World Plugs). Bring an adapter if your devices use a different plug.

faq.question: Is Switzerland in the EU or the Schengen Area?
faq.answer: Switzerland is not an EU member, but it is part of the Schengen Area through association agreements, so the same short-stay visa rules apply as in the EU Schengen states. For goods, the UK FCDO says there are strict rules about what you can take into and out of Switzerland, and you must declare anything that may be prohibited or subject to tax or duty.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Switzerland?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit Switzerland and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, they will need to obtain this online authorization (€20) before travel.

faq.question: How much does a Switzerland Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa fee is €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11; children under 6 pay nothing. Where the application goes through an external service provider, as at most Swiss representations, its service fee is added. The visa allows stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries.

faq.question: Do I have to declare cash when entering Switzerland?
faq.answer: There is no obligation to declare cash on entry, unlike in the EU. However, if you carry CHF 10,000 or more (or equivalent), customs officers can require you to disclose your identity and the origin, intended use and beneficial owner of the money — refusing or lying is a customs offense.

faq.question: Do I need a vignette to drive in Switzerland?
faq.answer: Yes — using Swiss motorways requires a vignette costing CHF 40, valid for 14 months (1 December of the previous year to 31 January of the following year), available as a windscreen sticker or an e-vignette registered to your plate. Driving on a motorway without one incurs a CHF 200 fine, and you must buy the vignette on the spot as well.
